title: Charge transport, generation & recombination
subtitle: How electrons and holes move (drift and diffusion), how light creates them, how they disappear again, and how far they get before they do.

skills: Read a slope: $\mathrm{d}n/\mathrm{d}x$ of a straight line is (change in n) / (distance), in cm⁻⁴
Keep every length in **cm** when densities are in cm⁻³ and D in cm²/s
Use Lambert–Beer from week 1: $\Phi(x) = \Phi_0 e^{-\alpha x}$
Solve $y'' = -c$ (a parabola) and $y'' = y/L^2$ (exponentials) with two boundary conditions

concepts.title: Drift: carriers pushed by an electric field
concepts.summary: Carriers always move randomly; an electric field adds a net drift velocity v = μξ. The drift current J = q(nμₙ + pμₚ)ξ, and the conductivity σ = q(nμₙ + pμₚ).

concepts.title: Diffusion: from crowded to empty
concepts.summary: Random motion alone moves carriers from high to low concentration. The diffusion current is proportional to the gradient: Jₙ = qDₙ dn/dx, Jₚ = −qDₚ dp/dx. The Einstein relation links D and μ: D = μk_BT/q.

concepts.title: Generation: light creates electron–hole pairs
concepts.summary: A photon with E ≥ E_G creates one electron–hole pair; the excess energy thermalises. The generation rate follows the absorption profile: G(x) = (1 − R)Φ₀α e^{−αx}.

concepts.title: Recombination: how carriers disappear
concepts.summary: Electron and hole annihilate and give their energy away: as a photon (radiative), to a third carrier (Auger), via a defect level in the gap (Shockley–Read–Hall) or via surface defects (surface recombination). Passivation reduces surface recombination.

concepts.title: Lifetime and diffusion length
concepts.summary: Under low injection every mechanism gives R = Δ/τ. Rates add, so 1/τ = Σ 1/τᵢ. A minority carrier diffuses a distance L = √(Dτ) before it recombines; L must be large compared with the cell for good collection.

sources.ref: Auger and radiative coefficients of c-Si: Dziewior & Schmid (1977); Trupke et al. (2003)
sources.note: Only used in the lifetime diagram.

concepts.title: The continuity equation: bookkeeping for carriers
concepts.summary: The carrier density at a point changes by what flows in, what is generated and what recombines. In steady state without a field this becomes D Δ'' − Δ/τ + G = 0, which gives the carrier profiles of book ex. 7.5, 7.7 and 7.8.

concepts.title: Putting it together: how a solar cell works
concepts.summary: Absorption and generation, transport without recombination, separation at the junction, collection at the electrodes. Week 3 supplies the middle steps; weeks 4–5 add the junction.

diagrams.title: Drift current and conductivity versus doping
diagrams.tryThis: Compare 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ phosphorus with 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ boron: same number of carriers, different conductivity. Then find the doping of book ex. 7.6(h).

diagrams.title: A concentration gradient drives a diffusion current
diagrams.tryThis: Load book ex. 6.14, then make the gradient twice as steep and watch the current double; flip to holes and see the sign change.

diagrams.title: Where light generates carriers
diagrams.tryThis: Compare 450 nm with 1000 nm: blue light generates almost everything in the first micrometre, infrared light deep in the wafer. Then load book ex. 7.5.

diagrams.title: Recombination mechanisms and the effective lifetime
diagrams.tryThis: Start with a clean wafer (SRH lifetime 1 ms) and raise the doping: find where Auger recombination takes over. Then add defects.

diagrams.title: Steady-state carrier profiles from the continuity equation
diagrams.tryThis: In book ex. 7.8, slide the surface recombination velocity from 0 to very large and watch the right end of the profile drop to zero.

notes.text: **Instruction 3 has no official answers yet.** All solutions to book ex. 7.6, 7.7 and 7.8 on this page are **self-derived, not official**. They are checked by independent computations (and the profiles of 7.7 and 7.8 by a numerical solver), but compare with the official answers when they appear.
**Book ex. 6.14 and 7.5 come from instruction 2** (week 2), but use lecture 3 material, so they are worked out here. Their official answers are in the answer book (ex. 6–7.5).

**Answer book ex. 7.5(c)–(e)** uses $e^{-\alpha x} = 5.3 \times 10^{-7}$ at 50 µm. With $\alpha = 2.90 \times 10^5$ m⁻¹: $e^{-14.5} = 5.0 \times 10^{-7}$. Their Φ(50 µm) = 1.14 × 10¹⁵ m⁻²s⁻¹, G = 3.3 × 10²⁰ m⁻³s⁻¹ and Δn = 4.1 × 10¹⁴ m⁻³ are therefore about 5 % high; consistent values are 1.08 × 10¹⁵, 3.1 × 10²⁰ and 3.9 × 10¹⁴. Both are accepted in the questions.

**Answer book ex. 6.15** computes the field from n = 10¹⁵ cm⁻³, the *lowest* density in the gradient. The electron density changes across the 2 µm, so the field that cancels diffusion is not uniform: at n = 2.7 × 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ it would be only 128 V/cm. The question is ambiguous; know where the 3468 V/cm comes from.

**Book ex. 7.8: boundary condition at x = 0.** The text says the minority carrier *concentration* is zero, n(0) = 0, so Δn(0) = −n₀. Many textbook versions say the *excess* concentration is zero, Δn(0) = 0. Because n₀ is tiny in p-type silicon (≈ 10⁴ cm⁻³), the two give practically the same profile. The self-derived solution keeps −n₀ in and shows both.

**Notation.** The lecture (slide 35) writes $R_{\mathrm{SRH}} = C_pN_T(p - p_0)$ with a capital C; the sheet (eq. 7.39) writes $c_pN_T(p-p_0)$, and keeps capital $C_n$, $C_p$ for the Auger coefficients (eq. 7.43). The lecture writes the continuity equation with $G_L + G_{th} - R_n$; the sheet (eq. 6.34) uses the *net* thermal rate $R_n$ and the external generation $G_n$. Same physics.

**Book p. 76** says lifetimes in c-Si solar cells ‘should be in range of tens of milliseconds’, just after calling 1 µs typical and ~1 ms the value for very pure material. That sentence looks inconsistent; don't memorise it. The lecture gives no target value.

**Lifetime diagram data (not in the course material):** Auger coefficients of c-Si $C_n = 2.8 \times 10^{-31}$ cm⁶/s and $C_p = 9.9 \times 10^{-32}$ cm⁶/s (Dziewior & Schmid, 1977), radiative coefficient $B = 4.73 \times 10^{-15}$ cm³/s (Trupke et al., 2003). They only serve to show trends; exam questions will give you any coefficient you need.

**Mobility is kept constant** at the sheet values (1360 and 450 cm²/Vs) in all diagrams. In reality it drops at high doping and high temperature (book p. 59); exercises give their own values (e.g. 1350 in ex. 6.15, 470 in ex. 7.6h, 1250 in the book example on p. 72).
